title: Why Herman Heunis Sold Mxit at Its Peak, and What Came After
dek: In 2011 the tired founder of Africa's biggest mobile chat network sold it and stepped away; four years later he watched it close.

story.event: Selling Mxit at its peak while burnt out, then seeing it decline and close
story.summary: In September 2011 Herman Heunis, who had built Mxit in Stellenbosch from the chat function of a failed SMS game, sold his entire stake, as did Naspers, to Alan Knott-Craig Jr's World of Avatar, saying it was time for new energy. Under new ownership Mxit cut about 40 of 150 jobs in 2012 and lost users to WhatsApp and other rivals; it shut its commercial operations in October 2015, giving its technology to The Reach Trust, and the app closed in 2016. Heunis tweeted in October 2015 that he had been too burnt out in 2011 to take Mxit further.
paragraphs: Early in 2011 Alan Knott-Craig Jr, a young Stellenbosch investor, sat in Herman Heunis's office and, near the end of a talk about local technology, raised the idea of buying Mxit. Heunis said he would think about it. He had built the chat service from the wreck of a mobile game that rising SMS prices had sunk. Cheap messaging on ordinary phones had since made Mxit Africa's largest mobile social network, with more than 43 million registered accounts in about 120 countries.

Heunis was tired. A 2012 profile said the idea of leaving had formed in 2007, during seven months of recovery after a motorbike accident that broke his back. The company now had 150 staff, and he did not think his real strength was running companies: "it is starting companies," he said. Knott-Craig later said he had first taken an interest after hearing of a falling-out between Heunis and Naspers, which had bought 30 per cent in 2007. In September 2011 Heunis and Naspers sold their entire holdings to Knott-Craig's World of Avatar, leaving 10 per cent with a staff trust Heunis had set up. "It is time to inject new and young energy into the company," Heunis said, and he took a six-month sabbatical.

The new owners struggled. Knott-Craig left in October 2012 after reportedly clashing with investors over strategy, and that December about 40 of the 150 staff were retrenched. WhatsApp, BlackBerry Messenger and Facebook drew users away. Mxit counted 2.7 million monthly active users in South Africa at the end of 2014, and 1.2 million in July 2015. On 23 October 2015 it shut its commercial operations and gave its technology to The Reach Trust, a public-benefit organisation, for education and social projects. The app itself closed in 2016.

Four days later Heunis posted his first tweet since January. "Pity I was so burntout in 2011 to take mxit further," he wrote, adding that the missing catalyst had been new energy. Since leaving he had ridden mountain-bike races, taken up wildlife photography and kitesurfing, and bought a run-down smallholding outside Cape Town.

quote.text: Defraud not thyself of a good day; and let not the portion of a good desire pass thee by. Shalt thou not leave thy labours unto another? and thy toils to be divided by lot?
quote.locator: Ecclesiasticus, chapter 14 (verses 14-15 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira reminds his reader that every labour passes to someone else sooner or later, and that a good day is not to be thrown away. Heunis handed Mxit on and used the days he got back; the company still did not survive, and the verse makes no promise that it would.

reflection: Heunis's tweet holds two things at once. He was too tired to carry Mxit further, and he wished he had not been. Neither cancels the other, and nothing in the record suggests that a rested Heunis would have held off WhatsApp.

Ben Sira's advice is not to waste a good day, because everyone's labours pass to someone else in the end. You cannot choose whether your work outlives your attention, only how you hand it on and what you do with the days you get back. Tiredness is worth hearing early, while there is still a choice about what to do with it.
invitation: Tonight, before you sleep, give your tiredness this week a number from one to ten and tell one person you trust what it is. Nothing else needs deciding today.

research_notes: The slate framed this as Heunis watching Mxit lose its users and close, but Heunis had sold the company four years before the closure, so the story centres on his documented decision to sell in 2011 and follows the company to its end. User numbers vary widely: 43 million registered accounts at the sale (TechCentral, Daily Maverick, Brainstorm; Brainstorm and HumanIPO say 128 countries, Daily Maverick 120); BizNews/Fin24 quotes Heunis on a peak of 42 million global users in 2011; iAfrikan says 50 million; Bizcommunity (2022) says 88 million at closure. The story uses the contemporary 43 million registered accounts and the company's own 2014 and 2015 monthly active user figures for South Africa. Registered accounts and active users are different measures and are not compared in the story. Price: undisclosed; the R500 million figure was called a rumour by Knott-Craig (Daily Maverick) and an industry estimate by Brainstorm, so it is not given. Founding: Daily Maverick dates Mxit's release to 2003 as part of a game's messaging platform, Business Report says the concept was conceived in 2003, and BizNews, Memeburn and iAfrikan say it was founded or launched in 2005; the story avoids a founding year. The 2007 motorbike accident and seven-month recovery rest on HumanIPO (which places it in 'the Zambian desert', an unclear location), so the story attributes it to a 2012 profile and gives no place. Heunis's remark about starting rather than running companies is quoted from HumanIPO, which presents it as his words at the time of the sale. The tension with Naspers rests on unnamed Memeburn sources and on Knott-Craig's own account to TechCentral of a 'fall-out', so it is attributed to Knott-Craig. Africa-ME quotes Heunis as calling the sale 'traumatic' and himself 'extremely tired and burned out', but no original source for that interview could be found, so it was not used. Final closure: iafrica.com (15 September 2016) quotes the notice to users that Mxit would close on 30 September 2016; Wikipedia gives 24 September; the story says only that the app closed in 2016. Heunis died in August 2022 aged 63 (Bizcommunity, citing MyBroadband); this is outside the episode and is not in the story. The Ben Sira verses are general counsel about using one's days and the certainty of leaving one's labours to others; they are applied here by analogy.
